newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks slide on fears of oil price hike.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks slide on fears of oil price hike.

text.p: Indian stocks fell in jittery trade on Friday after new Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral reminded investors he could not avoid raising the prices of petroleum products, traders said.

Gujral told state-run Doordarshan television in an interview on Thursday that he would need the nation's support and confidence in tackling the huge oil pool deficit, which totalled 155 billion rupees ($4.32 billion) by the end of 1996/97 (April-March).

"You cannot go on living with this kind of deficit that you are soon reaching a stage where you do not have the money to buy. I do not want to reach that stage," Gujral said, adding that a decision on the issue was unavoidable.
The oil pool deficit is the subsidy the federal government owes to state-run oil companies for selling their products well below international prices.
Gujral's statements drove investors to the sidelines and dampened market enthusiasm over the return of free-market reformer P. Chidambaram as finance minister.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index was trading 15.88 points, or 0.41 percent, lower at 3825.23 by 0840 GMT but up from its early low of 3803.03.
"Gujral's statement has weakened the market. But there is not much action," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the affiliate of Goldman Sachs & Co.
On the National Stock Exchange (NSE), the index fell 10.05 points, or 0.97 percent, to 1069.35.
Analysts said the timing of the petroleum product price hike remained uncertain.

"The unavoidability of any policy decision, especially on oil does not necessarily translate into an immediate price hike," said an analyst at a European brokerage, pointing out that an "imminent" hike in prices has been expected for several months.
"Looking at the current political situation, a price hike looks difficult," he said, referring to a corruption scandal involving a ruling party leader.
The federal police have said they would prosecute the chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, Laloo Prasad Yadav, in a scandal centred on illegal diversion of animal welfare funds.
Yadav, who is the president of Gujral's Janata Dal party, says he is innocent but has refused to accept opposition demands that he must step down and face trial.
"The decision on the timing will be taken by the Prime Minister. It is always done very secretively to avoid dealers building inventories," the analyst added.
